title: How do you prevent SQL injection in a .NET application?
description: Parameterized queries, ORM usage, dynamic identifier whitelisting, and least-privilege databases.

data.text: **Question:** How do you prevent SQL injection in a .NET application?

Never build SQL by concatenating untrusted input. Use parameterized commands (ADO.NET `SqlParameter`, EF Core LINQ or interpolated `FromSql`, Dapper parameters) so the database engine always treats input as **data**, not code. Parameters cannot fix dynamic identifiers (`ORDER BY` columns), so whitelist those against a fixed list. Defense in depth: give the app's login only the privileges it needs.

**How the attack works:**
- Input like `' OR '1'='1` closes the string literal and adds a condition that is always true → every row returns
- Stacked statements (`'; DROP TABLE Users;--`) execute extra commands when multiple statements are allowed
- Injection also reaches into `LIKE`, `ORDER BY`-adjacent logic, and even XML/JSON SQL functions
- The bug is in how the query is *assembled*, not in what the input "looks like"

**Prevention layers:**
- **Parameterized queries** — the plan is compiled once; input can never change query shape
- **EF Core LINQ** — expressions translate to parameters automatically
- **Interpolated raw SQL** (`FromSql($"... {value}")`) — the compiler turns `{value}` into a parameter
- **Never** format/concatenate into `FromSqlRaw`, `SqlCommand`, or Dapper SQL
- **Whitelist dynamic identifiers** — column names and sort directions cannot be parameters; map allowed values explicitly
- **Least privilege** — the app's SQL login should not own the schema or hold DDL rights, so a successful injection still cannot `DROP TABLE`
- Input validation and WAFs are additional layers, not substitutes for parameters

data.title: Vulnerable vs safe data access

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Muscle memory for parameters over string building
- Knowing that ORMs are not automatically safe (formatted raw SQL bypasses them)
- Awareness of the identifier-whitelisting gap that parameters leave open
- Defense-in-depth thinking: database privileges as a second wall

items: Believing stored procedures make concatenated input safe — they don't
Sanitizing input with quotes/keywords instead of parameterizing
Assuming EF Core protects you, then passing formatted strings to FromSqlRaw
Building ORDER BY / table names from request values without a whitelist
Running the app as a sysadmin-grade SQL login, so one injection owns the server
Using AddWithValue with implicit conversions as a habit — prefer typed parameter adds for predictable plan behavior
How do parameterized queries actually work below the API (precompiled plans)?
How would you hunt for injection risks in a legacy codebase?
Second-order injection: what is it and why does parameterizing the input still matter later?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Concatenated input = SQL injection; parameters make input data, not code
EF Core LINQ and interpolated FromSql parameterize automatically
Whitelist dynamic identifiers — ORDER BY columns can't be parameters
Least-privilege database accounts limit the blast radius
data.takeaway: Parameterize every value, whitelist every identifier, and give the database login only what it needs — layered defenses survive one mistake.
